summary: Discovery call for private VPC deployment. Crestwood runs financial risk models and needs a private deployment in their AWS account with strict data residency and KMS controls. Key asks: VPC peering or PrivateLink, support for cross-account peering, private endpoints, region restrictions (no EU data leaving London), SOC2 compliance, SSO/SAML, audit logs retention, and options for hybrid dedicated capacity. Redwood AE/SE covered architecture options, fallback behavior to hosted in burst scenarios, and next steps for network diagram and bench testing.
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-03-04
- Time: 15:00 PT
- Duration: ~57 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Laura Chen (Crestwood Head of Platform), Ethan Moore (Crestwood Security), Priya Kapoor (SRE), Samir Das (CTO)

Summary (auto): quick discovery re: private VPC setup, peering, private endpoints, KMS, region constraints.

00:00 Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. i'm jordan, account exec at redwood, with marcus our se. quick round robin?
00:10 Laura: laura here — i run the platform team at crestwood. we own infra for the risk models.
00:14 Ethan: ethan, security engineer. i'll be focused on encryption, audit logs, sso stuff.
00:18 Marcus: hi all, marcus from redwood, i'll get into the networking bits.
00:22 Jordan: great — objective today is just to understand your constraints and walk through private vpc options — peering vs privatelink/private endpoint and what we need for a dedicated deployment.
00:40 Samir: high level — we process sensitive financial predictions and need zero public egress for data, also we have a requirement that eu workloads stay in eu-west-2 (london) region.
00:52 Priya: we also want to avoid cross-account over-open rules, so ideally peering with routes only to redwood subnets, or AWS PrivateLink.
01:08 Marcus: got it. redwood private supports two primary modes for private: 1) customer-managed VPC peering/cross-account peering to our serving subnet, 2) PrivateLink / interface endpoints where we publish an ENI in your account and traffic never traverses the public internet. both can meet your no-public-egress requirement depending on config.
01:35 Laura: what's the operational difference? e.g. do we need to manage NAT or route table changes?
01:42 Marcus: for peering you will add a peering connection and update route tables to send traffic to the redwood subnets; no NAT required. for private link we create an endpoint service on our side and you create an interface endpoint — thats more control on your end for security groups but it's per-az and can add cost.
01:58 Ethan: are you doing cross-account peering, like our account -> redwood account? we have strict SCPs and limited iam privileges.
02:06 Jordan: yes, we do cross-account peering. typical pattern is customer creates peering on their side and accepts on redwood side; we provide a terraform snippet. we also support an alternative where redwood publishes an endpoint service and you accept that.
02:28 Ethan: any gotchas re: overlapping CIDR spaces? we can't renumber large subnets.
02:33 Marcus: overlapping CIDRs are the classic gotcha — for peering they must not overlap. for PrivateLink you can avoid that because traffic goes to an ENI; however you still need to plan security groups and route tables. we often recommend a small /24 for the redwood interface in your VPC if using PrivateLink.
02:55 Laura: latency is important; our 99th percentile for risk scoring calls needs to be under 300ms. what are your numbers for dedicated vs hosted?
03:08 Marcus: for dedicated GPU pools we typically see p99 in the 50-200 ms range depending on model and sequence length; hosted public endpoints add a tiny bit more network overhead. if you deploy in the same aws region as your workloads we can hit your target with batching defaults tuned for latency.
03:30 Samir: region question — we need all eu data processed and stored in eu-west-2. can you guarantee region pinning?
03:38 Jordan: yes — private deployments can be provisioned in a specific region and we can restrict routing such that models and KV caches run in that region only. for dedicated capacity we map a customer to capacity in the requested region.
03:49 Ethan: what about key management? we need to use our own KMS (customer-managed CMKs) and HSM for PKI, no key material in redwood's account.
03:58 Marcus: we support customer-managed KMS keys for data at rest and integration with BYOK flows. for private deployments you can bring your KMS and we will encrypt model caches with your CMK; we'll need an IAM role for decrypt access scoped to the instances. we can support HSM-backed keys via AWS CloudHSM when part of an enterprise contract.
04:20 Priya: audit logs — retention 7 years for certain finance regs — can you stream audit logs to our s3 or kafka?
04:29 Jordan: yes — we have configurable audit streaming. for private we can forward audit events to your S3 bucket, or to your SIEM via Kinesis or a Kafka connector. retention and lifecycle policies are up to you.
04:45 Ethan: ok, security questionnaire — we will want SOC 2 plus iso27001 documentation, penetration test reports, that sort of thing.
04:53 Jordan: we are SOC 2 Type II and have ISO certs — i'll drop our security pack. also we have a running list of pen test summaries — i'll include that.
05:05 Laura: what about network egress — if redwood needs to reach out for model downloads or updates, does that ever come from our VPC?
05:15 Marcus: model onboarding happens through a signed artifact flow; for private deployments we can stage model artifacts in your S3 or pull from a pre-authorized bucket in our account via a cross-account role. but by default runtime traffic doesn't egress to public internet unless you opt-in for model pulls.
05:34 Samir: in a failover scenario — say your region is down, do you have a fallback to hosted multi-region? we need to understand cross-region failover and data residency implications.
05:45 Marcus: good question — our default is regional fail-open policies are controlled by you. we can set a strict policy that disallows routing to other regions; alternately you can allow an A/B fallback to a pre-approved region but that means data could leave. for finance regs we usually recommend a dedicated DR runbook that keeps data in-region and relies on customer-managed replication for backups.
06:10 Ethan: is it possible to do a hybrid — private VPC for production, and hosted for non-prod or burst?
06:15 Jordan: absolutely — customers often do prod in private/dedicated and use hosted for dev/test/burst. we also support auto-burst policies where requests beyond dedicated capacity get routed to a hosted variant; that is configurable and can be blocked entirely if you want.
06:33 Priya: cost implications? PrivateLink costs per ENI and data processed, peering is cheaper but operationally heavier.
06:40 Marcus: correct — peering is lower long-term L3 data transfer cost but requires CIDR planning. PrivateLink has per-hour endpoint charges per AZ and scales differently. we'll include a cost comparison spreadsheet in the follow-up.
06:58 Laura: okay, show me a rough onboarding plan and timeline. we have a Q2 timeline for PoC, need to demo by mid-april.
07:06 Jordan: for a PoC we'd propose: week 1 — network prep and security questionnaire; week 2 — private endpoint or peering setup; week 3 — run benchmark tests with your test corpus; week 4 — iterate and tune; goal to have a short pilot by end of april.
07:25 Samir: that's reasonable. i'll need to get legal and procurement involved — any standard terms for private deployments?
07:33 Jordan: we have an enterprise addendum for private and dedicated with SLAs — i'll surface standard terms and a sample SOW.
07:40 Ethan: about SSO — we need SAML and SCIM provisioning into our Okta.
07:45 Marcus: supported; we can integrate SAML for the console and SCIM for user provisioning. for API auth you can use mTLS, API tokens, or a private auth gateway in your VPC.
08:00 Laura: Can you send a terraform snippet we can use to automate peering?
08:04 Jordan: yes — i'll share templates for both peering and PrivateLink plus an example route table and security group Terraform.
08:12 Marcus: also i will include a sample iptables/egress rule set we typically recommend for hardened deployments.
08:20 Ethan: curious — how do you handle KV cache encryption and purge? we need guaranteed purge on customer request and retention logs.
08:29 Marcus: KV cache is per-customer; for private deployments we ensure the KV cache is scoped to your cluster and encrypted with your CMK. purge API is available and we can provide attestations and deletion logs.
08:44 Priya: any limitations on model sizes or quantization that might affect memory footprint on dedicated nodes?
08:51 Marcus: our serving runtime supports model sharding and quantized weights; for larger models we recommend dedicated GPU types and we can advise on quantization profiles. we'll capture your expected sequence lengths and concurrency to propose VM types.
09:10 Laura: ok i'm convinced this is feasible — next step for us is internal network review, security questionnaire and to pick a preferred region list.
09:20 Jordan: perfect — action items and i'll send the security pack, architecture diagram, terraform snippets, pricing sheet, and schedule the benchmarks call.
09:30 Samir: thanks everyone — quick note, please mark EU data residency as a must and ensure any fallback plans are explicitly opt-in.
09:36 Jordan: noted.

Transcript end.
